```{webr}
#| include: false
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_gray(base_size = 14))
squad <- read.csv("data/jump_squad.csv")
balance <- read.csv("data/balance.csv")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## In this lesson you will learn to
- control axes with `scale_x_continuous()` / `scale_y_continuous()`: limits, breaks and label formats,
- **zoom** correctly with `coord_cartesian()` (and why `limits` can silently change your results),
- choose **colour-blind-friendly** colours with `scale_colour_manual()` and viridis palettes,
- write informative **labels with units**.

⏱️ About 40 minutes.
:::

## What is a scale?

Every aesthetic (`x`, `y`, `colour`, `fill`, `size`, …) has a **scale** that translates data values into something visible: positions, colours or sizes. ggplot2 picks a sensible default scale, but you can override it by adding a `scale_<aesthetic>_<type>()` function:

| Function | Controls |
|---|---|
| `scale_x_continuous()`, `scale_y_continuous()` | numeric axes |
| `scale_x_discrete()` | categorical axes (order, labels) |
| `scale_colour_manual()`, `scale_fill_manual()` | your own colours for categories |
| `scale_colour_viridis_d()`, `scale_colour_viridis_c()` | viridis palettes (discrete / continuous) |
| `scale_x_log10()` | logarithmic axis |

## Axes: breaks, limits and labels

```{webr}
ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 130, by = 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0.20, 0.60, by = 0.05))
```

- `breaks` sets where the tick marks are,
- `labels` changes how they're written, e.g. `labels = function(x) x * 100` to show metres as centimetres. The **scales** package (installed with ggplot2) has ready-made formatters such as `scales::percent`.

### Zooming: `limits` vs. `coord_cartesian()`

There are two ways to zoom in, and they are **not** the same:

- `scale_y_continuous(limits = c(a, b))` **removes** all data outside the limits *before* any calculation,
- `coord_cartesian(ylim = c(a, b))` keeps all data and just zooms the view, like a camera.

The difference matters for anything ggplot2 calculates: box plots, smoothing lines, means. Compare:

```{webr}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.35, 0.45)) +
  labs(title = "limits: data outside 0.35-0.45 m are DELETED")

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.35, 0.45)) +
  labs(title = "coord_cartesian: same boxes, just zoomed")
```

The first plot gives a warning (*"Removed … rows"*) and its medians and boxes are **wrong**: they're calculated only from the remaining athletes.

::: {.quiz id="m33-q1"}
You want to zoom in on part of a scatter plot that has a regression line (`geom_smooth(method = "lm")`). What should you use?

- [ ] `scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)`
- [x] `coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)`
- [ ] Either: the result is identical

::: {.explanation}
With `limits`, the points outside the range are removed and the regression line is refitted on fewer data, so it changes! `coord_cartesian()` only zooms the view.
:::
:::

::: {.task}
Make a scatter plot of `body_mass_kg` (x) against `jump_height_m` (y), but show the y-axis in **centimetres**: use `scale_y_continuous()` with `breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05)` and `labels = function(x) x * 100`. Label the axes with `labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (cm)")`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_1
#| caption: "Exercise · Axis breaks and labels"
ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = ______, labels = ______) +
  labs(x = "______", y = "______")
```

::: {.hint exercise="m33_1"}
`breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05)`, `labels = function(x) x * 100`, and the axis titles from the task.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="m33_1"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_1
#| solution: true
ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0.25, 0.55, by = 0.05), labels = function(x) x * 100) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (kg)", y = "Jump height (cm)")
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_1
#| check: true
p <- .result
res <- .check_plot(p, geoms = "GeomPoint")
if (isTRUE(res$correct)) {
  sc <- p$scales$get_scales("y")
  if (is.null(sc) || !is.function(sc$labels)) res <- .no("Add `labels = function(x) x * 100` inside `scale_y_continuous()`.")
  else if (!isTRUE(all.equal(sc$labels(0.4), 40))) res <- .no("The label function should multiply by 100.")
  else if (!identical(p$labels$y, "Jump height (cm)")) res <- .no("Set the y-axis title to \"Jump height (cm)\" with `labs()`.")
  else res <- .ok("Correct! The data stay in metres, but readers see centimetres.")
}
res
```

## Colours

### Choose colours for everyone

About **1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women** have some form of colour-vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling **red from green**. ggplot2's default palette isn't designed for this, and red/green combinations are the worst choice.

Two safe options:

1. The **Okabe–Ito** palette, designed to be distinguishable for all common types of colour blindness:

```{webr}
okabe_ito <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000")
```

2. **viridis** palettes (`scale_colour_viridis_d()` for categories, `scale_colour_viridis_c()` for numbers), which are colour-blind friendly, print well in grey-scale and are *perceptually uniform*: equal steps in the data look like equal steps in colour.

`scale_colour_manual(values = ...)` assigns your own colours to the categories. A **named** vector makes sure each category always gets the same colour:

```{webr}
sport_cols <- c(Basketball = "#E69F00", Soccer = "#0072B2")

ggplot(squad, aes(x = body_mass_kg, y = jump_height_m, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = sport_cols)
```

For a **numeric** variable mapped to colour, use a continuous viridis scale:

```{webr}
ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_time_s, y = con_force_rel, colour = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Jump\nheight (m)")
```

(`\n` starts a new line in a title.)

::: {.task}
Make box plots of `peak_power_rel` per `sport`, with `fill = sport`. Colour the boxes with `scale_fill_manual()` using the named vector `sport_cols` (given), and hide the redundant legend with `show.legend = FALSE` in `geom_boxplot()`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_2
#| caption: "Exercise · Manual colours"
sport_cols <- c(Basketball = "#E69F00", Soccer = "#0072B2")

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel, fill = sport)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = ______) +
  ______(values = ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="m33_2"}
`show.legend = FALSE` and `scale_fill_manual(values = sport_cols)`. Use the **fill** version because the boxes use `fill`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="m33_2"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_2
#| solution: true
sport_cols <- c(Basketball = "#E69F00", Soccer = "#0072B2")

ggplot(squad, aes(x = sport, y = peak_power_rel, fill = sport)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = sport_cols)
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_2
#| check: true
p <- .result
res <- .check_plot(p, geoms = "GeomBoxplot", aes = "fill")
if (isTRUE(res$correct)) {
  if (!grepl("scale_fill_manual", paste(.user_code, collapse = ""), fixed = TRUE))
    res <- .no("Use `scale_fill_manual(values = sport_cols)`. With `scale_colour_manual()` only the outlines would change.")
  else res <- .ok("Correct! A consistent, colour-blind-friendly colour per sport. Reuse `sport_cols` in every figure of your report.")
}
res
```

::: {.quiz id="m33-q2"}
Which colour combination should you avoid for two groups?

- [x] Red and green
- [ ] Orange and blue
- [ ] Black and light grey

::: {.explanation}
Red–green colour-vision deficiency is by far the most common type. Orange/blue (as in Okabe–Ito) is a safe pair.
:::
:::

## Ordering categories

Categories appear in **alphabetical order** by default. For ordinal data that's wrong, and for nominal data a meaningful order (e.g. by the median) makes plots easier to read. Change the order by setting the factor levels ([lesson 1.3](m1-03-factors.qmd)), or use `reorder()` to sort categories by a statistic:

```{webr}
balance$activity <- factor(balance$activity, levels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High"))

ggplot(balance, aes(x = reorder(fear_falling, fes_total, FUN = median), y = fes_total)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Fear of falling (sorted by median score)", y = "FES-I score")
```

## Labels with units

Every axis title of a scientific figure should state **the quantity and its unit**: "Jump height (cm)", not "jump_height_m". `labs()` sets all titles in one go:

```{webr}
ggplot(squad, aes(x = peak_power_rel, y = jump_height_m * 100, colour = sport)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Basketball = "#E69F00", Soccer = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(
    x = "Peak power (W/kg)",
    y = "Jump height (cm)",
    colour = NULL,                       # no legend title needed here
    title = "Peak power and jump height",
    subtitle = "84 professional athletes, countermovement jump",
    caption = "Each point is one athlete."
  )
```

You can transform data directly inside `aes()`: `y = jump_height_m * 100` plots centimetres without changing the data frame.

For special notation, R understands **plotmath** expressions: `labs(y = expression("Force (N·kg"^-1*")"))` gives a superscript. Plain text such as "N/kg" or Unicode characters ("m·s⁻¹") are often simpler.

::: {.task}
Complete the plot of `con_time_s` (x) against `con_force_rel` (y), coloured by `jump_height_m` with `scale_colour_viridis_c()`. Add labels: x = `"Propulsion time (s)"`, y = `"Mean propulsive force (N/kg)"`, colour = `"Jump height (m)"`.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_3
#| caption: "Exercise · Viridis and labels"
ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_time_s, y = con_force_rel, colour = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  ______() +
  labs(x = "______", y = "______", colour = "______")
```

::: {.hint exercise="m33_3"}
`scale_colour_viridis_c()`, then the three labels exactly as given in the task.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="m33_3"}
```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_3
#| solution: true
ggplot(squad, aes(x = con_time_s, y = con_force_rel, colour = jump_height_m)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = "Propulsion time (s)", y = "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)", colour = "Jump height (m)")
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: m33_3
#| check: true
p <- .result
res <- .check_plot(p, geoms = "GeomPoint", aes = "colour")
if (isTRUE(res$correct)) {
  if (!grepl("viridis", paste(.user_code, collapse = ""))) res <- .no("Add `scale_colour_viridis_c()`.")
  else if (!identical(p$labels$x, "Propulsion time (s)") || !identical(p$labels$y, "Mean propulsive force (N/kg)"))
    res <- .no("Check the axis titles: they should match the task exactly.")
  else res <- .ok("Excellent! The colour gradient shows how jump height depends on force AND time together. You'll model exactly this with multiple regression in Module 4.")
}
res
```

::: {.quiz id="m33-q3"}
Which axis title is best for a scientific figure?

- [ ] `peak_power_rel`
- [ ] `Power`
- [x] `Peak power (W/kg)`

::: {.explanation}
A good axis title names the quantity in words and gives its unit. Column names are for code, not for readers.
:::
:::

## Lesson summary

- `scale_x/y_continuous(breaks = , labels = )` controls ticks and their format.
- Zoom with `coord_cartesian()`; `limits` deletes data and changes computed statistics.
- Use colour-blind-friendly colours: Okabe–Ito with `scale_colour_manual(values = c(Group = "#hex", ...))`, or `scale_colour_viridis_d()` / `_c()`.
- Order categories with factor levels or `reorder()`.
- Axis titles = quantity + unit, set with `labs()`.
